theory.overview: Activation functions are the gatekeepers of neural networks. They decide whether a neuron should 'fire' (activate) or not, introducing non-linearity into the network. Without activation functions, no matter how many layers you stack, your neural network would behave like a simple linear model—incapable of learning complex patterns. Each activation function has unique characteristics: some are smooth and differentiable everywhere (sigmoid, tanh), some are computationally efficient (ReLU), and some solve specific problems like vanishing gradients.

sections.title: Why We Need Non-Linearity
sections.content: Imagine trying to separate a spiral dataset with a straight line—impossible! Real-world data is rarely linear. Activation functions allow neural networks to learn curved decision boundaries, approximate any continuous function (Universal Approximation Theorem), and capture complex relationships. Without them, stacking 100 linear layers is mathematically equivalent to having just 1 linear layer.
keyPoints: Linear functions compose to linear functions: $f(f(x))$ is still linear
Without activation functions, deep networks have no advantage over shallow ones

sections.title: Sigmoid: The Classic S-Curve
sections.content: The sigmoid function squashes any input to a value between 0 and 1, making it perfect for probability outputs. It was the go-to activation for decades, but has fallen out of favor for hidden layers due to the vanishing gradient problem—when inputs are far from zero, gradients become nearly zero, stopping learning.

sections.title: Tanh: Zero-Centered Sigmoid
sections.content: Tanh is essentially a scaled and shifted sigmoid that outputs values between -1 and 1. Being zero-centered helps with training dynamics—gradients can flow in both positive and negative directions more naturally. It's often preferred over sigmoid for hidden layers, but still suffers from vanishing gradients.

sections.title: ReLU: The Modern Default
sections.content: ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) is beautifully simple: if input is positive, output it; otherwise, output zero. This computational efficiency and avoidance of vanishing gradients for positive values made it the default choice for hidden layers. However, it has a fatal flaw: the 'dying ReLU' problem where neurons can permanently turn off.

sections.title: Leaky ReLU & Variants
sections.content: To solve the dying ReLU problem, variants allow a small negative slope. Leaky ReLU uses a small constant (typically 0.01), PReLU learns this slope, and ELU smooths the negative region exponentially. These modifications prevent neurons from permanently dying while keeping most of ReLU's benefits.

sections.title: Softmax: For Multi-Class Output
sections.content: Softmax is special—it's designed for output layers in classification tasks. It converts raw scores (logits) into a probability distribution where all outputs sum to 1. The exponential ensures the winner takes more probability mass, while the denominator normalizes everything.
sections.intuition: Emphasizes the largest value, suppresses smaller ones

keyConcepts.name: Vanishing Gradients
keyConcepts.description: When gradients become extremely small during backpropagation, preventing weight updates. Common with sigmoid/tanh in deep networks.
keyConcepts.solution: Use ReLU, batch normalization, or residual connections

keyConcepts.name: Exploding Gradients
keyConcepts.description: When gradients become extremely large, causing unstable training with huge weight updates.
keyConcepts.solution: Gradient clipping, careful initialization, batch normalization

keyConcepts.name: Dead Neurons
keyConcepts.description: ReLU neurons that always output 0 because they're stuck in the negative region.
keyConcepts.solution: Use Leaky ReLU, lower learning rates, or better initialization

keyConcepts.name: Saturation
keyConcepts.description: When activation function outputs reach their min/max bounds, gradients become near-zero.
keyConcepts.example: Sigmoid outputs near 0 or 1 have almost no gradient

steps.title: Input Values
steps.description: Activation functions transform the weighted sum before passing it forward.
steps.latex: z = w \cdot x + b$ is the input to activation function

steps.title: Apply Sigmoid
steps.description: Squash the input to range (0, 1). Notice how large negative values approach 0 and large positive values approach 1.

steps.title: Apply Tanh
steps.description: Squash to range (-1, 1). Zero-centered output helps with training.

steps.title: Apply ReLU
steps.description: Simply pass through positive values, block negative values.

steps.title: Compare Gradients
steps.description: The derivative tells us how much the output changes with input—crucial for learning.

steps.title: Softmax for Classification
steps.description: Convert raw scores to probabilities that sum to 1.

practiceProblems.title: Sigmoid Calculation
practiceProblems.explanation: At x=0, sigmoid outputs 0.5. Positive inputs push toward 1, negative toward 0.

practiceProblems.title: ReLU Behavior
practiceProblems.description: For inputs $x = [-2, -1, 0, 1, 2]$, what are the ReLU outputs?
practiceProblems.explanation: ReLU outputs 0 for all negative inputs and passes positive values through unchanged.

practiceProblems.title: Softmax Temperature
practiceProblems.description: Given logits $[2.0, 1.0, 0.0]$, compute softmax. What happens if you multiply all logits by 2? By 0.5?
practiceProblems.explanation: Higher temperature (×2) makes distribution more 'peaked' (confident). Lower temperature (×0.5) makes it more uniform.

practiceProblems.title: Gradient Flow Analysis
practiceProblems.description: A neuron has input $z = 10$. Compare the gradients for sigmoid and tanh.
practiceProblems.explanation: Both suffer from vanishing gradients far from origin, but sigmoid's max gradient is 0.25 while tanh's is 1.0.

practiceProblems.title: Dying ReLU Analysis
practiceProblems.description: A ReLU neuron has weights that produce negative output for ALL training examples. What happens during training?
practiceProblems.answer: The neuron 'dies'—gradient is always 0, weights never update, neuron stays inactive forever.
practiceProblems.explanation: This is the 'dying ReLU' problem. Since ReLU's gradient is 0 for negative inputs, no learning occurs. Solutions: Leaky ReLU, careful initialization, or lower learning rate.
hints: Gradient of ReLU for negative inputs is 0
No gradient means no weight updates

practiceProblems.title: Choosing Activations
practiceProblems.description: Design a network for: (a) Binary classification, (b) Multi-class classification with 10 classes, (c) Regression predicting house prices.
practiceProblems.answer: (a) Sigmoid output, ReLU hidden | (b) Softmax output, ReLU hidden | (c) Linear/no activation output, ReLU hidden
practiceProblems.explanation: Output layer choice depends on task: binary (sigmoid), multi-class (softmax), regression (linear). Hidden layers typically use ReLU.
